extracted_claim: British Airways reports just under 50,000 flights and more than 2.5 million passengers flown supersonically; it lists a 1,350 mph (2,160 km/h, Mach 2) cruise and withdrawal of service in October 2003.
what_it_supports: sustained direct evidence that a Mach 2-class civil passenger service operated at meaningful scale
what_it_does_not_support: a current service, a universal airport/noise/energy solution, or any speed class above Mach 2

extracted_claim: NASA states that the Tu-144 was one of only two first-generation SSTs to enter production and commercial service; passenger service began in November 1977 and ended in 1978 after 102 passenger flights.
what_it_supports: a second direct airline-passenger precedent and evidence that service duration and scale must be reported
what_it_does_not_support: a durable commercial business case, present-day practicality, or a faster-than-Mach-2 passenger anchor

extracted_claim: NASA describes the later Tu-144LL as a former first-generation jetliner modified into a flying laboratory for supersonic research; its 1996-1999 flights were research flights, not passenger service.
what_it_supports: why research-aircraft flight evidence must not be counted as scheduled passenger-service evidence
what_it_does_not_support: commercial service, passenger acceptance, certification, or a new service-speed anchor
